rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
Arrange the following compounds in increasing order of their property as indicated in bracket : (Any two)
(i) \(\mathrm{CH_3-CHO,\ CH_3-CO-CH_3,\ CH_3-CO-C(CH_3)_3}\)
(reactivity towards HCN)
(ii) \(\mathrm{CCl_3-COOH,\ CF_3-COOH,\ (CH_3)_3C-COOH}\)
(acid strength)
(iii) 2,4-Dinitrobenzoic acid, 4-Nitrobenzoic acid, 4-Methoxybenzoic acid, Benzoic acid
(acid strength)
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - parts (i) and (iii) are DRAWN rather than written. (i) draws the three carbonyls with explicit vertical C=O bonds and a vertical tert-butyl branch on the third; (iii) draws four benzene rings - inner alternating double bonds clearly present at 3x zoom, so genuinely aromatic, unlike the plain hexagon in Q6(b)(iii) - bearing COOH plus, respectively, NO2 at C-2 and C-4, NO2 at C-4, OCH3 at C-4, and nothing. Both are READ losslessly into the stem (condensed formulas for (i), IUPAC names for (iii)), which is safe here because naming states none of the answer: what the question asks for is the ORDER, not the identity. The same naming was used for the equivalent drawn rings on committed sibling 2022 56/5/1 Q2. Page idx 2.
rows.solution:
(i) Increasing reactivity towards hydrogen cyanide:
\(\mathrm{CH_3{-}CO{-}C(CH_3)_3} < \mathrm{CH_3{-}CO{-}CH_3} < \mathrm{CH_3{-}CHO}\)

Nucleophilic addition begins with cyanide attacking the carbonyl carbon, so reactivity falls as that carbon is made less positive and more crowded — and every alkyl group does both, releasing electron density inductively and physically blocking the approach.

Ethanal has ONE alkyl group there; propanone has TWO. The first compound is worst of all: besides having two alkyl groups it carries a bulky TERT-BUTYL group, which shields the carbonyl carbon almost completely.

(ii) Increasing acid strength:
\((\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{C{-}COOH} < \mathrm{CCl_3{-}COOH} < \mathrm{CF_3{-}COOH}\)

Acid strength is decided by the stability of the carboxylate anion, and anything WITHDRAWING electron density spreads the charge and stabilises it.

The TERT-BUTYL group does the reverse, RELEASING density, so that acid is the weakest. Both halogenated acids are much stronger, three halogens withdrawing powerfully — and FLUORINE, the more electronegative, withdraws more than chlorine, so trifluoroacetic acid is strongest of all at \(\mathrm{pK_a}\) 0.23 against trichloroacetic acid's 0.66.

(iii) Increasing acid strength:
4-METHOXYBENZOIC ACID < BENZOIC ACID < 4-NITROBENZOIC ACID < 2,4-DINITROBENZOIC ACID

The METHOXY group donates a lone pair into the ring, raising the electron density and WEAKENING the acid. The NITRO group withdraws, both inductively and by resonance, and STRENGTHENS it. TWO nitro groups withdraw more than one, and the 2,4-compound has the advantage of one of them being ORTHO, close enough to act inductively at short range.

rows.stem: Define conductivity for the solution of an electrolyte. Why does the conductivity of a solution decrease with dilution ?
rows.solution:
CONDUCTIVITY, \(\kappa\), is the conductance of a solution held between two electrodes ONE CENTIMETRE APART with an area of ONE SQUARE CENTIMETRE — in other words, the conductance of a UNIT VOLUME of the solution. It is the reciprocal of resistivity:
\(\kappa = \dfrac{1}{\rho} = \dfrac{1}{\mathrm{R}}\left(\dfrac{l}{\mathrm{A}}\right)\), with units \(\mathrm{S\ cm^{-1}}\)

IT DECREASES ON DILUTION because the number of IONS PER UNIT VOLUME falls.

What carries the current through that fixed block of solution is the ions inside it. Diluting spreads the same ions through a larger volume, so the block now holds fewer of them and conducts less. The degree of dissociation does rise on dilution, but for a strong electrolyte that offers nothing further — it is already complete — and even for a weak one the rise does not keep pace with the fall in concentration.

Note that MOLAR conductivity behaves in the OPPOSITE way and INCREASES on dilution, because it counts the conductance furnished by a fixed AMOUNT of electrolyte — one mole — rather than by a fixed volume. The two quantities are related by \(\Lambda_m = \kappa/\mathrm{C}\), and they move in opposite directions for exactly that reason.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
Account for the following :
(i) \(\mathrm{Cr^{2+}}\) is a strong reducing agent.
(ii) \(\mathrm{Ti^{3+}}\) is coloured whereas \(\mathrm{Sc^{3+}}\) is colourless in aqueous solution.
(iii) Zn, Cd and Hg are not called transition elements.
rows.solution:
(i) Because \(\mathrm{Cr^{2+}}\) reaches a stable configuration by GIVING UP an electron.

Chromium(II) is \(3d^4\). Losing one more electron gives \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\), which is \(3d^3\) — in an octahedral aqueous environment the stable HALF-FILLED \(t_{2g}^3\) arrangement, with one electron in each of the three lower orbitals.

A species that gives up an electron readily IS a reducing agent, and chromium(II) does so eagerly: \(E^{\circ}\) for the couple is \(-0{\cdot}41\) V, negative enough that chromium(II) reduces even water and liberates hydrogen.

(ii) Because titanium(III) has a d ELECTRON and scandium(III) has none.

Colour arises from a D-D TRANSITION: a ligand field splits the five d orbitals into two sets, and an electron absorbs visible light to jump from the lower set to the upper. The jump needs an electron below and a vacancy above.

\(\mathrm{Ti^{3+}}\) is \(3d^1\) — one electron, plenty of vacancies — so its solutions are violet. \(\mathrm{Sc^{3+}}\) is \(3d^0\), with the argon configuration and no d electron at all, so no such transition is possible and its solutions are colourless.

(iii) Because their d subshells are COMPLETELY FILLED in both the atom and the ion.

A transition element is defined as one with a PARTLY FILLED d subshell in the neutral atom or in at least one stable ion. Zinc, cadmium and mercury are \(d^{10}\) as atoms AND \(d^{10}\) as their \(+2\) ions, so neither condition is met.

The consequences are all negative ones: white and diamagnetic compounds, a single \(+2\) oxidation state, poor catalytic activity, and unusually low melting points — mercury being liquid at room temperature.

rows.stem: What is Lanthanoid contraction ? What is the cause of Lanthanoid contraction ? Write two consequences of Lanthanoid contraction.
rows.solution:
LANTHANOID CONTRACTION is the steady DECREASE in atomic and ionic radii across the lanthanoid series, from lanthanum to lutetium, despite the increase in atomic number.

THE CAUSE is POOR SHIELDING by the \(4f\) ELECTRONS.

Each element added along the series brings one more proton to the nucleus and one more electron to an inner \(4f\) orbital. But \(f\) orbitals are diffuse and badly shaped for screening, so they shield the outer electrons from the nucleus poorly. The effective nuclear charge felt by the outer shells therefore GROWS at every step, and they are pulled inwards.

The contraction is small at each step but CUMULATIVE, amounting to about 20 pm across the fourteen elements.

TWO CONSEQUENCES:

ZIRCONIUM AND HAFNIUM HAVE ALMOST IDENTICAL RADII, about 160 pm each, although hafnium lies a whole period lower — the fourteen lanthanoids intervening between them cancel the increase expected from the extra period. The two behave so alike that they occur together and are notoriously difficult to separate.

THE LANTHANOIDS THEMSELVES ARE DIFFICULT TO SEPARATE, being so close in size and almost all in the \(+3\) state, so that ion-exchange or solvent extraction must be used instead of ordinary chemical methods.

A third consequence: the BASIC CHARACTER of the hydroxides decreases steadily from \(\mathrm{La(OH)_3}\) to \(\mathrm{Lu(OH)_3}\), as the shrinking ion holds the hydroxide more tightly.
